results.title: CI/CD and Quality Assurance in Software Testing | xMatters
results.content: So how can we make sure that our quality assurance framework covers full integration testing and still supports smaller sets of tests that may overlap without repeating code across services during the CI/CD process? We still need to be able to execute the test suites by service and have the test results feed back into that service’s CI/CD pipeline so that we can easily detect defects and monitor trends in defect analysis (more on this later). For quality assurance, we created a new shared pipeline code that executes integration tests in parallel (to speed up the overall execution time of the pipeline), collates the results, and provides a single report for the multiple suites that are executed as part of that pipeline. The Allure Framework tool shows a concise representation of this data in a web report form, allowing us to use a single tool for reporting no matter what service is being tested, and easily integrates the test results to Test Case Management tools like TestRail and defect management tools like JIRA.

results.title: An example of reproducibility checking when data is restricted-access - Office of the AEA Data Editor
results.content: # An example of reproducibility checking when data is restricted-access I wanted to highlight a recently (2020-04-30) published article in the AEJ:Economic Policy as an example of reproducibility checking when data is restricted-access. Overall, the report received from the 3rd party replicator was useful confirmation that the code that anybody can see would work well on the data that few people can see, and materially improved the replication package. Take-away message: While we cannot do reproducibility checks on restricted-access data in a timely fashion for all papers that use restricted-access data, there are still many opportunities to do so, and we will always attempt to do so. The AEA Data and Code Availability Policy asks that authors provide access to all data used in a published paper.

results.title: Domain Naming for Dev/Test/Prod: Structure for CI/CD in 2025 |
results.content: # How to Design Domain Naming Conventions for Dev/Test/Prod Environments. Clear, consistent domain naming for development, testing, and production environments isn’t just about staying organized; it’s about enabling automation, reducing human error, and maintaining infrastructure hygiene. One of the most common issues with domain naming is reusing production names for test or dev environments. Lastly, avoid embedding environment data deep in path structures, like example.com/api/dev/v1. When provisioning new test branches or ephemeral dev sites, a naming system like pr-[number].service.dev.example.com allows full automation. Structuring your naming to use \*.dev.example.com allows you to deploy and secure many subdomains under one cert without constant reissuance. For internal dev or testing environments, use private TLDs like .internal, or restrict access via firewalls and VPNs. Still, the naming convention should remain consistent. In an age where everything from staging environments to SSL certs is automated, a consistent and clear DNS naming pattern is more than just good hygiene, it’s a competitive advantage.

Cloud Data Security AI-Powered Threat Detection for Cloud Storage. + **Singularity Cloud Security Posture Management** Detect and Remediate Cloud Misconfigurations. # What are CI/CD Tools? | How to Choose CI/CD Tool? Continous integration (CI) and continuous deployment (CD) tools allow teams to merge, build, test, and deploy code branches automatically. Once you commit to using CI/CD in your software development cycle, you’re immediately faced with a galore of options: Travis, Jenkins, GitLab, CodeShip, TeamCity, and CircleCI, among others. Think about your operating systems and their versions, programming languages, access to third-party APIs, libraries, frameworks, and testing suites; collect all these data and check that each tool is able to support them all. * If you’re building .NET projects to run on a Microsoft stack, you’ll find two natural choices: **Visual Studio Team Services (VSTS)**and **TeamCity.** Both include Docker support. * Extra charges from CI/CD cloud services come in the form of higher concurrency, build events, build time, and/or user count. * Some cloud services have a zero-cost plan for small teams. * On-premises options like GitLab, Travis-CI, and TeamCity have hosted offerings that let you test before committing to run your own copy. * On-premises tools require resources ready to orchestrate your builds and tests. * Teams should be aware of legal and business requirements when uploading code and data to cloud services. It’s only a matter of time before the results of using CI/CD become visible to management. * Provide some managers read access to your CI/CD. * need training for more than your vanguard CI/CD team. Don’t forget to consider how much effort it would take your team to migrate your delivery pipeline to a different tool or provider in case a change is necessary. * How tightly integrated is your CI/CD tool to specific computing resources? If your current software development cycle is made of stages where people step on each others’ toes while trying to survive the minefield created by libraries, APIs, and interservice dependencies, perhaps it’s time to choose a CI/CD tool and start optimizing your software delivery pipeline.

results.title: CI/CD testing strategies for data pipelines
results.content: # CI/CD testing strategies for data pipelines. ## Why data pipelines require a specialized testing approach. Data pipeline development presents unique challenges for software testing. Unlike traditional applications, data pipelines must handle varying data volumes, complex transformations, and strict quality requirements while maintaining performance and reliability. Testing data pipelines requires specialized attention because:. * **Processing guarantees** – Exactly-once processing and late-arriving data handling need thorough verification. * **Compliance requirements** – PII handling, GDPR requirements, and retention policies demand rigorous testing. ## Key testing strategies for data pipeline CI/CD workflows. * **Schema validation** – Test schema evolution, nested structure handling, and type conversions. * **NULL handling** – Validate missing data in joins, default values, and NULL propagation. * **Data quality checks** – Test referential integrity, business rules, and value constraints. * **Contract testing** – Verify data contracts, primary/foreign keys, and uniqueness constraints. * **Reference data** – Test consistency with master data, lookup tables, and historical versions. * **Incremental loads** – Test delta processing, CDC handling, and state management. * **Throughput testing** – Measure processing speed and validate partition strategies. * **Concurrency handling** – Test parallel processing and resource contention scenarios. Modern data stacks require careful integration testing. * **Source validation** – Test API integrations, CDC processes, and file ingestion patterns. * **Downstream systems** – Test BI tools, ML pipelines, and API endpoint consistency. * **Recovery testing** – Verify checkpoint restoration and idempotent processing. * **Monitoring integration** – Test metric collection, alerting thresholds, and SLA tracking. * **State management** – Validate checkpoint data, temporary storage, and cleanup processes. * **Version control** – Test dependency management and backward compatibility. * **Data protection** – Validate encryption, PII handling, and secure transformations. * **Compliance checks** – Test regulatory requirements and governance policies. Data pipeline development requires continuous testing and validation. * **Automate validation** – Run dbt tests, Great Expectations suites, and custom quality checks. * **Environment isolation** – Test with production-like data volumes and systems. * **Custom tooling** – Integrate specialized testing frameworks and monitoring tools. * **Scale testing** – Handle large-scale data validation efficiently. * **Cache effectively** – Optimize test data and dependency management. * **Quality gates** – Test data quality and transformation accuracy. * **Secure testing** – Protect sensitive data during validation.
